newsitem.title: TAIWAN: With rivals' blessings, Taiwan-China sailing looms.
newsitem.headline: With rivals' blessings, Taiwan-China sailing looms.

text.p: Taipei said on Thursday the first direct sailings of the Taiwan Strait since 1949 could take place within 10 days, now that rival China has approved five mainland shippers to pioneer the Taiwan-China service.
Taiwan's transportation ministry said it expected to receive applications from the five newly authorised China firms within a few days and would approve them swiftly.
"The ministry will be able to process the mainland shippers for cross-strait links in less than a week after receiving them," transport vice minister Mao Chi-kuo told reporters.

Ting Chan-neng, head of the ministry's navigation and aviation section, said direct crossings could begin as soon as 10 days from Thursday if, as expected, the mainland firms' paperwork is received within two or three days.
"They can start right away," Ting said.

Beijing on Wednesday approved five state-run shippers to start the service and said it was processing applications from a dozen Taiwan shippers eager to ply long-forbidden cross-straits routes from the Nationalist-ruled island.

Taiwan has banned all direct contacts with China since 1949, when it was split from the newly communist mainland by a civil war. Cross-strait trade and investment nonetheless has flowered since a political thaw began in the late 1980s, most of it routed via Hong Kong.
The booming economic unofficial ties have created huge pressure for an easing of the shipping ban.
In February, with both governments' tacit approval, shippers from Taiwan and China reached a deal to do just that, although many conditions would still apply.
The crossings would link only the southern Taiwan port of Kaohsiung and the closest mainland port, Xiamen, a "special economic zone" in southeastern Fujian province.

Taiwan says Kaohsiung can receive ships sailing from China as long as they are owned by mainland, Taiwan or Hong Kong interests and fly the flag of Hong Kong or a third country -- not communist China's red five-starred flag.
In addition, Taipei refers to the service as "offshore transshipment" rather than direct shipping because mainland cargoes will not be allowed to enter Taiwan customs.
Mainland cargoes can be processed in an "offshore" bonded zone in Kaohsiung outside of customs for onward shipment.
Taiwan's conditions seek to ensure the breakthrough does not undermine the sovereignty of its exiled Republic of China, which has never recognised the communists' sovereignty.

Beijing, which regards Taiwan as a renegade province that must be unified with the mainland, has issued rules defining cross-straits shipping as a domestic matter and specifying that only Taiwan or China companies -- or joint ventures including one side or the other -- would be allowed to ply the routes.

The mainland firms found qualified by Beijing include major national line China Ocean Shipping and four Fujian firms: Fujian Provincial Shipping Co, Xiamen Shipping Co, Mawei Shipping Co, Fujian Foreign Trade Centre Shipping Co.
On the Taiwan side, analysts said Yangming Marine Transport Corp, Uniglory Marine, Wan Hai Lines, and Chinese Maritime Transport Ltd were front-runners to make the first direct crossings.
Local media said Uniglory was planning an April 25 inaugural ceremony. Uniglory would not confirm or deny the report.
Yangming has said it was preparing ships for a twice-weekly Kaohsiung-Xiamen service but would not comment further on Thursday.
